subject: Scam Alert #1: your package isn't really on hold
preheader: Fake delivery texts, marketplace "payment pending" emails, and a free checker for anything you're not sure about.
html:
Fake delivery texts, marketplace "payment pending" emails, and a free checker for anything you're not sure about.

Hi,

Black Friday is next week, which means two things: everyone is waiting on a package, and everyone is buying and selling on marketplaces. Scammers plan for both.

This week's scam: the "package on hold" text

Spotted this week (fictional example): "USPS: Your package is on hold due to an incomplete address. Update your details within 12 hours or it will be returned: usps-redeliver-●●●●.top/track. A $0.30 redelivery fee applies."

The thirty cents isn't the point. The page wants your name, address and card number, and once you've typed them in, the charges that follow aren't thirty cents.

The tell

A delivery text you didn't sign up for, with a link and a fee. Carriers don't text you out of the blue asking for an address update or money. And the link isn't the carrier's real site: read the part right before the first single slash.

What to do

  1. Don't tap. Track the package with the tracking number from the shop's own order email or app.
  2. Already entered card details? Call your card issuer now and cancel the card.
  3. Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM), then delete it.

Quick hits

  • Selling gifts on Marketplace? If an email says a buyer's payment is "pending" until you upgrade to a business account, it's fake. Payment apps don't charge you to receive money. Check the app itself.
  • Buying a sold-out gift? Never send a deposit by payment app to "hold" an item you haven't seen. Meet in person or use a checkout with a credit card.
  • Black Friday deal from a site you've never heard of? Search the shop's name plus "scam" or "reviews" before you pay, and pay by credit card so you can dispute it.

Bookmark our free Is this a scam? checker. Paste in any text, email or link you're unsure about, and it lists the red flags and what to do. It runs on your own phone or computer, so nothing you paste is sent anywhere. Send it to the person in your family who gets the most texts.

subject: Scam Alert #2: thanks for a donation you never made
preheader: Fake charity texts after Giving Tuesday, the boss who needs gift cards, and a 5-second check at the gift card rack.
html:
Fake charity texts after Giving Tuesday, the boss who needs gift cards, and a 5-second check at the gift card rack.

Hi,

Giving Tuesday was this week, and the year-end giving season runs to December 31. It's also the busiest time of year for gift cards. Scammers love both, because they're generous habits that move money fast.

This week's scam: the "thanks for your pledge" text

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Thank you for your generous pledge last year! Families in need are counting on you again this season. Renew your $75 gift today by gift card or Zelle: holiday-relief-●●●●.xyz"

You don't remember the pledge, but you don't want to seem stingy either. That doubt is the trick. There's no pledge and no charity.

The tell

Pressure to give today, by gift card, payment app, wire or crypto. Real charities welcome your gift next week too, and they take credit cards and checks.

What to do

  1. Look the charity up yourself. Check it at Give.org or Charity Navigator, and use the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search if you want the tax deduction.
  2. Give on the charity's own website, by credit card or check.
  3. Already paid? Call your card issuer or payment app now, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Quick hits

  • Your "boss" texts asking for gift cards for the team: they can't talk, they want photos of the codes, and they want it kept quiet. Walk to their desk or call their real number. It's a scam every time.
  • Buying gift cards as presents? Check the packaging isn't torn and the PIN isn't scratched or re-stuck, or buy from behind the counter. Keep the receipt with the card.
  • Paid a scammer with a gift card? Call the gift card company right away, using the number on the card or its website, and ask for a refund. The faster you call, the better your chances.

Your 5-minute job this week

Tell one older relative the rule that covers half of all holiday scams: gift cards are for gifts. Anyone who asks you to pay with one, for anything else, is a scammer. Our gift card explainer is short enough to forward.

subject: Scam Alert #3: the shop that only exists in your feed
preheader: Fake shops in social media ads, the 70% off that never ships, and how to check a store in 2 minutes.
html:
Fake shops in social media ads, the 70% off that never ships, and how to check a store in 2 minutes.

Hi,

Two weeks before the holidays, the ads in your feed get very good at guessing what you want. Some of those shops don't exist.

This week's scam: the store that only exists in an ad

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Last chance! Our warehouse is closing. Everything 70% off, today only. Free shipping on orders over $49. Shop now at the link."

The site looks polished, the photos are lifted from real brands, and checkout works fine. What arrives is a cheap copy, or nothing, and the 'customer service' email never answers.

The tell

A shop you'd never heard of until an ad, a price that's too good, and a countdown. Real closing-down sales don't need a timer on every page.

What to do

  1. Search the shop's name plus "scam" or "reviews" before you pay, and look for a real address and phone number.
  2. Pay with a credit card, which lets you dispute the charge if nothing arrives. Avoid payment apps, wires and gift cards.
  3. Already paid and nothing came? Call your card issuer and dispute it, then report the shop at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Quick hits

  • "Your order can't ship, confirm your card": if the email doesn't come from the shop you actually used, ignore it and check your order in the shop's own app.
  • Gift card deals on resale sites: cards sold at a big discount are often stolen or drained. Buy from the store or the brand.
  • Package texts are still peaking. Track from the shop's own order email, never from a link in a text. Our delivery text explainer has the full list.

Your 5-minute job this week

Before your next holiday order, check one thing: is the card saved in your shopping accounts a credit card, not a debit card? If something goes wrong, it's the bank's money on the line while they sort it out, not yours.

Not sure about a shop's text or email? Paste it into our free scam checker. It runs on your device and sends nothing anywhere.

Stay safe, Scam Decoded

subject: Scam Alert #4: the scam talk, minus the lecture
preheader: Going home for the holidays? A 30-minute plan to scam-proof your parents, and a canceled-flight text to ignore.
html:
Going home for the holidays? A 30-minute plan to scam-proof your parents, and a canceled-flight text to ignore.

Hi,

If you're heading home next week, you'll be at the same table as the people scammers call most. That's the best chance all year for a short, useful conversation.

This week's scam: the canceled flight text

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Your flight has been canceled due to weather. Call our rebooking desk at 1-888-555-0161 to secure a new seat before they're gone."

The number doesn't go to the airline. A friendly 'agent' charges a rebooking fee and takes your card, and your new ticket never appears. Scammers also buy search ads for airline help lines and reply to people complaining on social media.

The tell

A rebooking number that came from a text, an ad or a stranger, not from the airline. Your real flight status is in the airline's own app.

What to do

  1. Check your flight in the airline's app or on the website you typed yourself.
  2. Need help? Use the number on your booking confirmation or in the app.
  3. Already paid a fake agent? Call your card issuer the same day and dispute the charge.

Quick hits

  • The scam talk with your parents: start with your own story ("I got the weirdest text this week…"), not a warning. Our free holiday conversation guide has the openers and a 30-minute plan.
  • Pick a family safe word while everyone's together. Anyone calling in a panic for money has to say it. No word, call them back.
  • Charity calls keep coming until December 31. Look the charity up yourself and give on its own website.

Your 5-minute job this week

Print the holiday guide and put it in your bag. Page 4 is a family plan you fill in together before you leave.

subject: Scam Alert #5: a short one for Christmas Eve
preheader: Gift card balance texts, new phones for parents, and one job for the week between the holidays.
html:
Gift card balance texts, new phones for parents, and one job for the week between the holidays.

Hi,

A short one today. If you're reading this on Christmas Eve, thank you, and close it after the first section if you've got cooking to do.

This week's scam: the gift card balance text

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Your gift card balance of $100.00 is about to expire. Verify your card number and PIN to keep your funds: giftcard-balance-●●●●.com"

If you got gift cards this year, expect a few of these. The page asks for the card number and PIN, and then the balance is gone.

The tell

A text or email about a gift card you didn't register anywhere. Card companies don't text you about expiring balances.

What to do

  1. Check a balance only on the website printed on the back of the card, or in the store's own app, typed in yourself.
  2. Never type a gift card's number and PIN into a page you reached from a text.
  3. Already did? Call the gift card company right away and ask them to freeze the card.

Quick hits

  • New phone for Mom or Dad? Before it's wrapped up for the night: turn on spam call filtering, install updates, and save their bank's real number as "BANK (real)".
  • Selling unwanted gifts? Meet buyers in person, get paid on the spot, and ignore emails saying a payment is "pending" until you upgrade your account.
  • "Merry Christmas from the IRS"? No. The IRS doesn't text or email you about refunds or penalties.

Your 5-minute job this week

Nothing this week. Enjoy the holidays.

Merry Christmas, Scam Decoded

P.S. Happy holidays, from all of us at Scam Decoded. See you next Thursday.

subject: Scam Alert #6: a 15-minute security reset for New Year's
preheader: Three things to lock before midnight, the subscription renewal email to ignore, and a resolution that works.
html:
Three things to lock before midnight, the subscription renewal email to ignore, and a resolution that works.

Hi,

Last issue of the year. Instead of a resolution you'll drop by February, here's one that takes 15 minutes and lasts all year.

This week's scam: the auto-renewal email

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Your annual protection plan has been renewed. $389.99 has been charged to your account. To cancel and get a refund within 48 hours, call 555-0193."

There's no plan and no charge. The number goes to a scammer who wants remote access to your computer, or your card details, to 'refund' you.

The tell

A charge you don't recognise, plus a phone number and a deadline. Check the real account or your card statement. No charge there means no charge.

What to do

  1. Don't call the number in the email.
  2. Check your card statement or log into the real account yourself.
  3. Already gave remote access? Disconnect from the internet, call your bank, and get the computer checked. Our fake order explainer has the full steps.

Quick hits

  • Shopping returns season: fake "return label" emails arrive in early January. Start every return from the shop's own app or order page.
  • New year, new number? If someone texts "Hi, this is my new number" and then asks for money, call their old number first.
  • Tax season starts soon. We'll cover it in January, but the short version: the IRS doesn't text, email or call first about money.

Your 5-minute job this week

The 15-minute reset: (1) change your email password to a long, unique one and turn on two-step sign-in; (2) freeze your credit at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion if you haven't; (3) turn on transaction alerts on every card.

Want the whole family plan on paper? The Family Scam-Proofing Kit is our own $9 printable kit, with a family meeting script, credit freeze trackers for everyone and a fridge card.

Happy New Year, Scam Decoded

subject: Scam Alert #7: the return label that isn't
preheader: Fake return and refund emails after the holidays, plus what to do with all those new devices.
html:
Fake return and refund emails after the holidays, plus what to do with all those new devices.

Hi,

The returns window is open, and so are the scammers who've figured out we're all expecting a refund this week.

This week's scam: the refund that needs your details

Spotted this week (fictional example): "We're sorry your return couldn't be processed. To receive your refund of $84.50, please confirm your card details here within 24 hours."

It looks like the shop you just returned something to. It isn't. The page takes your card number and login, and the 'refund' never comes.

The tell

A refund that needs you to do something through a link. Real refunds go back to the card you paid with, automatically.

What to do

  1. Check the return's status in the shop's own app or order page.
  2. Never enter card details to receive a refund.
  3. Already did? Call your card issuer and change that account's password.

Quick hits

  • New devices: set up a passcode, turn on automatic updates and Find My, and use a unique password for the account the device signs into.
  • Smart speakers and doorbells: change the default password and keep the app updated.
  • Old phone you're giving away? Sign out of every account and do a factory reset first.

Your 5-minute job this week

Pick the one account that resets all the others, your email, and check where it's signed in. Sign out of any device you don't recognise.

Stay safe, Scam Decoded

P.S. Got a fake refund email this week? Reply and forward it to me (delete your personal details first).

- New devices: set up a passcode, turn on automatic updates and Find My, and use a unique password for the account the device signs into.

- Old phone you're giving away? Sign out of every account and do a factory reset first.

Pick the one account that resets all the others, your email, and check where it's signed in. Sign out of any device you don't recognise.

subject: Scam Alert #8: the new-year job that pays you to like videos
preheader: Task scams aimed at January job hunters, recruiter texts, and the one rule for any job offer.
html:
Task scams aimed at January job hunters, recruiter texts, and the one rule for any job offer.

Hi,

January is the busiest month for job hunting, and for job scams. If you or someone you know is looking, this one's for you.

This week's scam: the task job

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Hi! I'm a recruiter with a digital marketing agency. We have flexible remote work, 60–90 minutes a day, rating products for $300–$800 daily. Interested?"

The first payouts are real, $20 or $40. Then your account goes 'negative', and you have to top it up, usually in crypto, to unlock your earnings. That money doesn't come back.

The tell

A job that asks you to pay, deposit or buy anything to get paid. Plus a recruiter you never contacted, offering big pay for little work, moving you to WhatsApp or Telegram.

What to do

  1. Don't reply. Look the company up yourself and apply on its real careers page.
  2. Never pay for training, equipment or 'unlocking' tasks.
  3. Already paid? Stop, even if they say one more deposit releases your money, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Quick hits

  • Interviews by text only: real employers do video or in person. Our job scam explainer lists the signs.
  • A check to buy your work laptop: it'll bounce, and you'll owe the bank what you sent the 'vendor'.
  • SSN before an offer letter: that's identity theft, not onboarding.

Your 5-minute job this week

Forward this to the person in your life who's job hunting right now. Ten seconds of yours could save them a lot.

subject: Scam Alert #9: the wrong number that wants to be friends
preheader: How a 'wrong number' text turns into a crypto investment, and the rule that ends it.
html:
How a 'wrong number' text turns into a crypto investment, and the rule that ends it.

Hi,

This one starts politely and takes weeks. By the time money comes up, it feels like a friendship.

This week's scam: the wrong number

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Hi Emma, are we still on for dinner Saturday? … Oh sorry, wrong number! You seem nice though. Where are you based?"

Weeks of friendly chat later, your new friend mentions how well they're doing on a crypto trading platform, and offers to show you. The app shows your balance growing. When you try to withdraw, there's a 'tax' or 'fee' to pay first.

The tell

Anyone you've only met online who brings up investing, especially in crypto, on a platform they chose. Fees to withdraw your own money mean there's no money.

What to do

  1. Don't invest through a link or app someone you met online sent you.
  2. Check any adviser or firm at Investor.gov, and talk to someone you trust before moving money.
  3. Already invested? Stop paying 'fees', and report it to the FBI at IC3.gov and the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Beware of 'recovery' services that charge to get it back.

Quick hits

  • Social media is where most of these start. In FTC data, losses to scams that began on social media were about eight times higher in 2025 than in 2020.
  • Deepfake ads with famous faces selling investments are fake. A famous face selling an investment in an ad is a classic sign of a scam.
  • Our investment scam explainer covers the whole pattern.

Your 5-minute job this week

Reply to no wrong-number texts this week. Delete and block. It's the cheapest scam protection there is.

Stay safe, Scam Decoded

subject: Scam Alert #10: Data Privacy Day: lock 3 doors in 10 minutes
preheader: Data breach notices, fake breach settlements, and three free locks for your identity.
html:
Data breach notices, fake breach settlements, and three free locks for your identity.

Hi,

Today is Data Privacy Day. Your information has almost certainly been in a data breach. That's not a reason to panic. It's a reason to lock the three doors that matter.

This week's scam: the fake breach settlement

Spotted this week (fictional example): "You may be owed up to $1,200 from a data breach class action settlement. Confirm your identity with your Social Security number to file your claim: breach-claims-●●●●.com"

Real breach settlements exist, and some really do pay out. But the fake ones copy their style and ask for your Social Security number or bank details up front.

The tell

A settlement or breach notice that asks for your Social Security number or a fee. Real claim forms come from a settlement administrator named in court papers, and you can find the case yourself.

What to do

  1. Search the settlement's name yourself, plus "settlement administrator", before you click anything.
  2. Never pay a fee to claim money.
  3. Already gave your SSN? Freeze your credit today and report it at IdentityTheft.gov.

Quick hits

  • Real breach letter? Change that account's password, turn on two-step sign-in, and watch for phishing that mentions the breach.
  • Tax season opens soon: an IRS Identity Protection PIN stops others filing a return with your SSN. Get one at IRS.gov.
  • Data brokers sell your address and phone number. Many let you opt out, one by one.

Your 5-minute job this week

Lock three doors: (1) freeze your credit at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion; (2) turn on two-step sign-in for your email; (3) put a PIN or passcode on your mobile carrier account, so nobody can move your number.

From Scam Decoded

Next week: tax season. The IRS isn't texting you, and we'll show you what they actually do.

Stay safe, Scam Decoded

P.S. Did a breach letter ever lead to something worse for you? Reply and tell me. Your story helps others spot it.

subject: Scam Alert #11: the IRS isn't texting you
preheader: Tax season's fakes are out. 1 rule beats all of them.
html:
Tax season's fakes are out. 1 rule beats all of them.

Hi,

Welcome to the first weekly Scam Alert: one scam, decoded, every Thursday. It's tax season, so the fake IRS is everywhere this week.

This week's scam: "verify your IRS account"

Spotted this week (fictional example): "IRS: Your online account has been suspended. Verify your identity within 24 hours to release your refund: [link]"

The link opens a perfect copy of the IRS sign-in page. It takes your login, then asks for a photo of your driver's license "to confirm it's you." With both, someone can file a return in your name or get into your real account.

The tell

The IRS doesn't text or email you out of the blue about refunds or your account. So any message like this is fake, however official it looks.

What to do

  1. Delete the link. To check your real account, type IRS.gov yourself.
  2. Already entered your details? Change that password now, and follow the steps at IRS.gov's identity theft page.
  3. Forward the text to 7726 (the free spam-reporting number), then report it at IRS.gov.

Quick hits

  • The arrest call: "There's a warrant, pay today with gift cards." The real IRS doesn't threaten arrest or demand a payment method. Hang up and report it at tigta.gov.
  • State refund texts: scammers copy your state's tax department too. Check your refund on your state's official .gov site.
  • Free tool: an IRS Identity Protection PIN stops anyone else filing a return with your Social Security number.

Your 5-minute job this week

Get your IRS Identity Protection PIN. Search "IRS IP PIN" and make sure the address is irs.gov, or go there directly. It's free, and it's one of the best anti-fraud tools the IRS has.

subject: Scam Alert #12: "send me a photo of the back of the card"
preheader: Valentine's week scams, and one conversation worth having with your teen.
html:
Valentine's week scams, and one conversation worth having with your teen.

Hi,

Valentine's Day is Sunday, which makes this one of the busiest weeks of the year for romance scammers. And Tuesday was Safer Internet Day, so there's one more conversation at the end worth having.

This week's scam: the gift card favor

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Babe I'm so embarrassed to ask. My card isn't working out here and I wanted to send you something for Valentine's. Could you grab 3 gift cards and send me a photo of the backs? I'll pay you back the second I'm home 💕"

After weeks of good-morning texts, it feels small. But that photo is the money: the number and PIN let them spend it in seconds, and it's almost impossible to get back.

The tell

Anyone you've only met online who asks for gift cards is a scammer. The FTC is clear on this. No exceptions, however real they feel.

What to do

  1. Say it kindly, once: "I don't send money or gift cards to anyone I haven't met in person. Let's video chat this week."
  2. Already sent one? Call the gift card company on the number on the card, right away, and keep the receipt.
  3. Report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

Quick hits

  • "Your Valentine's gift couldn't be delivered": a $1.99 "redelivery fee" text is after your card number. Ask the sender, or check the carrier's own app.
  • The deployed soldier: if an online partner "needs" $2,500 for leave papers, it's a scam. The US Army says soldiers don't pay to go on leave.
  • The package stuck in customs: if they "shipped you something" and a courier wants fees, there is no package.

Your 5-minute job this week

Send one message to a teen in your life: "If anyone online ever threatens you with a photo, come to me. I won't be angry, and we'll fix it together." Criminals who run sextortion count on kids being too scared to tell anyone. The FBI says don't pay, save the messages and report it. For under-18s, NCMEC's free Take It Down tool helps get images removed. If anyone feels unsafe, call or text 988.

Forward this to one person dating online right now.

The Scam Decoded team

P.S. Know someone whose online partner "keeps sending them things"? Forward them this issue, with no lecture attached.

subject: Scam Alert #13: a refund you didn't expect (and a call to "send it back")
preheader: Why a scammer would send YOU money, and what to do instead.
html:
Why a scammer would send YOU money, and what to do instead.

Hi,

This week's scam is backwards: it starts with someone sending you money.

This week's scam: the "send it back" refund

Spotted this week (fictional example): A $3,140 deposit labeled "IRS TREAS 310 TAX REF" lands in your account. Two days later a caller says: "That refund was issued in error. Return it to our collection partner today or you'll face penalties."

Someone used your stolen details to file a fake return, and the refund went to your real bank account. If you "send it back" where they say, the money's gone and you still owe the IRS.

The tell

The IRS doesn't call to demand you send a refund to a third party. A refund you didn't file for is a sign someone filed in your name.

What to do

  1. Don't send money anywhere a caller, email or letter tells you to.
  2. Call your bank, and follow the IRS's own steps for returning an erroneous refund (IRS Tax Topic 161 on IRS.gov).
  3. Report identity theft through IRS.gov, freeze your credit, and get an IP PIN for next year.

Quick hits

  • "Settle your tax debt for pennies on the dollar": the FTC warns some tax relief companies charge big fees up front. Check IRS payment plans and the free Taxpayer Advocate Service first.
  • Your tax software is stuck? Don't call a number from a search result. Use the help button inside the software.
  • Real IRS letters have a notice number in the corner. Look it up on IRS.gov's "understanding your notice" page.

Your 5-minute job this week

Sign in to your IRS online account (type IRS.gov yourself) and look around. Knowing what your real account looks like makes the fakes easier to spot.

Forward this to whoever does the taxes in your family.

The Scam Decoded team

P.S. Owe the IRS and feeling stressed about it? You're not alone. We made a calm video about the free options on our YouTube channel this Sunday.

subject: Scam Alert #14: "Hi Mom, this is my new number"
preheader: 6 texts from hello to a $1,900 bill, and the 2-minute fix.
html:
6 texts from hello to a $1,900 bill, and the 2-minute fix.

Hi,

This one goes to parents more than anyone, so if you're the adult child, forward it up the family tree.

This week's scam: the new number text

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Hi Mom, dropped my phone in the sink 🙄 this is my new number, save it and delete the old one x" ... (small talk) ... "Are you free? I have a bill due today and I can't log into my banking on this phone. Could you pay it and I'll send it back tomorrow?"

Every step is believable on its own. Phones break, bills are due. And "delete the old number" stops you calling the real one.

The tell

A new number, plus an urgent payment, plus "I can't talk right now." That combination is the scam.

What to do

  1. Call the old number anyway. It almost always still works.
  2. Or ask a question only your child would know, or use your family safe word.
  3. If it really is them, they can wait five minutes. Real family always can.

Quick hits

  • "Unpaid tax on your payment app transactions": real 1099-K forms come from the app itself. Tax is paid through IRS.gov, never a text link.
  • AI voice clones: the same scam now comes as a phone call that sounds like your child. A safe word beats it too.
  • The QR code in a package you didn't order: don't scan it. You can keep the item.

Your 5-minute job this week

Pick a family safe word tonight: something silly and memorable, never posted online. Text it to your family group in person or by phone call, not in a group chat that could be hacked. Anyone asking for money in a hurry has to say it.

preheader: Slam the Scam Day: 6 government imposters and the one rule that beats them.
html:
Slam the Scam Day: 6 government imposters and the one rule that beats them.

Hi,

Today is Slam the Scam Day, run by Social Security's inspector general to fight government imposter scams. (Check ssa.gov for the confirmed date each year.) So this issue is a field guide.

This week's scam: "your Social Security number has been suspended"

Spotted this week (fictional example): "This is the Social Security Administration. Your Social Security number has been suspended due to suspicious activity in Texas. Press 1 to speak to an officer."

The "officer" says your number was used in a crime, and the only way to protect your savings is to move them to a "safe account" today.

The tell

Social Security numbers don't get suspended. And no real agency will ever tell you to move your money to protect it.

What to do

  1. Hang up. If you're worried, call Social Security on the number from its official website.
  2. Never move money, buy gift cards or hand cash to a courier because of a call.
  3. Report it at oig.ssa.gov.

Quick hits: what the real agencies won't do

  • IRS: won't threaten arrest or demand gift cards. It usually starts with a letter.
  • Medicare: won't call asking for your Medicare number. Cards are free.
  • Courts: don't call to collect fines for missed jury duty.
  • The FTC: won't call to "protect your money" or say you're under investigation.
  • Your utility: won't demand gift cards, crypto or a store barcode to stop a shutoff.

Your 5-minute job this week

Agree on one family rule: we never pay anyone who called, texted or emailed us first. We hang up and call the real number ourselves. Then practice one line with your parents: "I don't do that on the phone. I'll call you back."

The Scam Decoded team

subject: Scam Alert #16: the half-price beach house
preheader: Spring break rentals, March Madness "sure wins", and the one way to pay for travel.
html:
Spring break rentals, March Madness "sure wins", and the one way to pay for travel.

Hi,

Spring break and March Madness land in the same week, and so do two scams that look like great deals.

This week's scam: the fake vacation rental

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Hi! The beach house is still free for spring break 😊 If you book directly with me instead of through the site I can take off the fees, just send the $600 deposit by Zelle today, I have two other families asking."

The photos are often copied from a real listing. Once you pay off the platform, there's no protection, and the house might belong to someone else entirely.

The tell

A host who wants you off the booking site and paying by payment app, wire, gift card or crypto. The FTC flags all four.

What to do

  1. Reverse search the listing photos and look up the address on a map.
  2. Keep every message on the booking platform.
  3. Pay only through the platform or with a credit card, which gives you dispute rights if it turns out to be fake.

Quick hits

  • "Sure-win" March Madness picks: nobody can promise wins. If a betting app wants a fee before you can withdraw, the winnings were never real.
  • "Your power will be cut off in 30 minutes": hang up and call the number on your bill. Small businesses get this one a lot.
  • Spring clean your passwords: reused passwords are how one breach becomes five hacked accounts. A password manager fixes that.

Your 5-minute job this week

Turn on two-step sign-in for your email account. It's the key that resets every other password you have, so it's the one to lock first.
